paragraphs: Optimization proxies are machine learning models that approximate the solutions produced by optimization procedures. Their purpose is to return feasible, nearly optimal answers for different problem inputs. This paper studies how to verify their quality by determining the worst optimality gap over the instance distribution: how far a proxy’s answer can fall short of the true optimum.

The authors propose a more compact mathematical formulation of this verification problem. They also introduce a gradient-based primal heuristic to help with its computation. Together, these changes offer significant computational benefits relative to the original formulation. The new formulation also broadens applicability to non-convex optimization problems, where the optimization landscape can be more complicated.

The paper demonstrates these benefits on large-scale DC Optimal Power Flow and knapsack problems. The contribution concerns assessing an optimization proxy’s solution quality, rather than merely measuring its typical predictive accuracy. A more tractable worst-case analysis helps characterize how much optimality the learned approximation may sacrifice across the instances being considered.
icml-2024-compact-optimality-verificatio.tldr: A compact verification formulation and gradient-based heuristic make it more practical to assess optimization proxies’ worst-case optimality gaps.

paragraphs: One-shot imitation learning aims to let an agent perform a task after seeing a single demonstration. A central difficulty arises when the environment changes after that demonstration. The demonstrated behavior may no longer fit the agent’s current situation, so successful imitation requires more than following the original sequence of actions.

Deep Demonstration Tracing addresses this problem with a demonstration transformer that encourages the agent to identify suitable states within the demonstration as execution unfolds. This gives the demonstration a more adaptive role in guiding behavior. The method also places one-shot imitation inside a meta-reinforcement-learning training framework, providing regularization for how policies behave in unexpected situations.

The authors evaluate the approach on a new navigation task suite and robotics tasks involving unforeseen environmental changes. DDT outperforms the existing one-shot imitation methods across all tasks evaluated. These results support the value of combining adaptive use of demonstration states with training aimed at generalization. The demonstrated advantage specifically concerns dynamic settings where the agent encounters situations absent from its example.
icml-2024-deep-demonstration-tracing-lea.tldr: Deep Demonstration Tracing helps agents adapt a single demonstration to unforeseen changes through demonstration attention and meta-reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a probability distribution has several important regions separated by large gaps. Conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods can explore one region without moving effectively to the others. This poor mixing is a practical problem in applications such as Bayesian inference and molecular dynamics, where samples need to represent multiple possible configurations.

Diffusive Gibbs Sampling introduces an auxiliary noisy distribution using Gaussian convolution. This smoothing creates connections between modes that are isolated in the original space. The sampler alternates between the original and noisy spaces using Gibbs sampling, making the auxiliary space part of the exploration process. A new Metropolis-within-Gibbs scheme further improves mixing during the denoising sampling step.

The authors report better mixing than leading alternatives, including parallel tempering, and substantially improved performance on Gaussian mixtures, Bayesian neural networks, and molecular dynamics tasks. The central idea is to use a noisy companion distribution to support movement between separated regions. Its reported benefits concern more effective exploration of multimodal distributions across these evaluated applications.
icml-2024-diffusive-gibbs-sampling-8e4f4.tldr: Diffusive Gibbs Sampling alternates between original and noise-smoothed distributions to improve exploration of distant probability modes.

paragraphs: A convincing explanation does not necessarily tell a person how a language model will behave. This paper asks whether a model’s explanation helps people predict its answers when the original input changes. That shifts attention from how reasonable an explanation sounds to how accurately it describes behavior across related situations.

The authors call this property counterfactual simulatability and introduce precision and generality metrics to assess it. They use language models to generate varied counterfactual inputs automatically. Explanations are then assessed by whether the expectations they support agree with the model’s actual responses. The evaluation covers leading language models, including GPT-4, on multi-hop factual reasoning and reward modeling.

The study finds low explanation precision and no correlation between precision and plausibility. An explanation can therefore sound persuasive while providing an unreliable basis for anticipating the model’s decisions. These findings suggest that simply optimizing human approval, as in a naive application of reinforcement learning from human feedback, may be insufficient to produce explanations that accurately characterize model behavior.
icml-2024-do-models-explain-themselves-c.tldr: Language-model explanations often fail to predict behavior on changed inputs, even when those explanations sound plausible.

paragraphs: Detectors of diffusion-generated images often lose accuracy when images come from a generator they have not encountered before. DRCT tackles this generalization problem through difficult training examples: generated images that closely resemble real ones. Its motivating idea is that learning to distinguish these subtle cases could also help identify more obvious generated images, potentially including outputs from other diffusion models.

The framework creates hard samples through high-quality diffusion reconstruction. It then uses contrastive training to guide detectors toward learning diffusion artifacts. DRCT is designed to enhance existing detectors, making the training procedure the central intervention rather than requiring a single specialized detector architecture.

The authors also introduce DRCT-2M, a million-scale evaluation dataset covering 16 types of diffusion models. In cross-set tests, detectors enhanced with DRCT achieve accuracy improvements exceeding 10%. These findings support the approach’s ability to improve transfer across evaluated data settings. The proposed connection between difficult examples and unseen generators remains a motivation supported by experiments, rather than a guarantee of detection for every future generator.
icml-2024-drct-diffusion-reconstruction-.tldr: DRCT improves generated-image detector generalization by training on realistic diffusion reconstructions with a contrastive objective.

paragraphs: A model trained to generate 3D shapes can reproduce the training data’s appearance while still producing structural defects. The paper focuses on topological artifacts, including broken legs, small holes, and unrealistic thin structures. It adds training objectives that directly address these aspects of shape structure in an implicit shape generator.

The approach uses persistence diagrams to represent topological information and pursues two goals. First, generated shapes should have a diagram distribution aligned with that of training shapes. Second, diagrams should vary smoothly between adjacent synthetic shapes. The authors learn a generator of persistence diagrams and align its outputs with diagrams from generated shapes, using a shape regularization term to accommodate discrete and continuous diagram variability.

A further smoothness loss on the diagram generator improves the behavior of distribution alignment. Experiments on ShapeNet show substantially better generalization than leading implicit shape generators. The contribution is a way to guide shape generation through structural information, complementing the usual fitting process with objectives that encourage plausible topology and smoother variation among generated shapes.
icml-2024-enhancing-implicit-shape-gener.tldr: Topological training losses improve implicit 3D shape generators by aligning structural distributions and encouraging smooth variation between generated shapes.

paragraphs: Multimodal federated learning lets clients with different kinds of data collaborate to improve their personal models while preserving data privacy. Existing approaches often require compatible architectural components so that corresponding model blocks can be aggregated. This becomes restrictive when clients need different architectures or different ways to combine image, text, audio, and video information.

FedMBridge addresses architecture-personalized multimodal federated learning, where local architecture design is unrestricted. It must handle two sources of variation together: differences in clients’ data statistics and differences in their neural network structures. The method uses a topology-aware hypernetwork as a bridge, designed to manage both forms of heterogeneity while sharing useful information efficiently.

Experiments across four simulations of this setting demonstrate the approach’s efficiency and effectiveness. The significance is that useful collaboration need not be organized solely around matching model blocks. By explicitly accounting for architectural differences alongside data differences, FedMBridge supports a more flexible form of multimodal federated learning in which clients can retain distinct local modeling strategies.
icml-2024-fedmbridge-bridgeable-multimod.tldr: FedMBridge uses a topology-aware hypernetwork to enable efficient collaboration among multimodal federated clients with different data and architectures.

paragraphs: A common way to explain a graph neural network is to find a smaller subgraph that preserves the original graph’s predicted label. However, removing graph structure can produce inputs very different from the graphs used in training. The model’s prediction on such a subgraph may then be unreliable, undermining the comparison used to judge the explanation.

This paper proposes generating proxy graphs for candidate explanatory subgraphs. The proxies are designed to resemble the training distribution while retaining the factors relevant to the explanation. A parametric method uses graph generators to construct them, and an information-theoretic training objective balances distributional compatibility with preservation of explanatory content.

Predictions on these generated proxies provide approximations to the labels associated with the explanatory subgraphs. Evaluations across multiple datasets show more accurate explanations. The approach matters because it addresses the reliability of the model queries underlying explanation, rather than treating every extracted subgraph as an equally valid input. It seeks to preserve the explanatory signal while avoiding the distribution shift caused by extraction.
icml-2024-generating-in-distribution-pro.tldr: Generated proxy graphs improve GNN explanations by preserving explanatory factors while staying close to the training-data distribution.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models can produce text that refers to objects unsupported by the visual input. HALC targets this object hallucination problem during decoding, the process that selects the model’s generated words. Its approach uses fine-grained visual information while considering both immediate token choices and the broader text being produced.

At the local level, an automatic focal grounding mechanism corrects hallucinated tokens as generation proceeds. At the global level, a specialized beam search procedure helps reduce object hallucinations while maintaining text quality. These two components connect detailed visual checking with the selection of longer candidate outputs, so the method addresses both individual errors and their effect on the overall response.

HALC is presented as a plug-and-play module for vision-language models and requires no additional training. Experiments across four benchmarks show that it reduces object hallucination and outperforms leading alternatives. The results support decoding as a useful intervention point: the method improves the use of available visual evidence while the model is composing its answer.
icml-2024-halc-object-hallucination-redu.tldr: HALC reduces object hallucinations without extra training by combining local visual grounding with global decoding search.

paragraphs: This paper studies factual errors in language models by examining their internal representations of context. The authors observe that correct generations tend to exhibit sharper context activations in the hidden states associated with input tokens than incorrect generations do. This is an association that can provide a useful signal during generation, rather than a rule that perfectly separates truth from error.

The method turns this observation into an entropy-based measure of sharpness across in-context hidden states. It incorporates the measure into decoding by adjusting the probability distribution used to select the next token. Internal context activity therefore becomes part of the mechanism guiding the generated response toward greater factuality and overall quality.

Experiments on Natural Questions, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, and TruthfulQA show consistent effectiveness, including gains of up to 8.6 absolute points on TruthfulQA. These results support the practical usefulness of the proposed signal. The work also offers an internal-representation perspective on hallucination, linking a measurable pattern in model activity to an intervention in text generation.
icml-2024-in-context-sharpness-as-alerts.tldr: An entropy-based signal from contextual hidden states helps adjust language-model decoding and reduce factual errors.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a deep neural network changes its representation as an input passes through successive layers. The authors want to track both newly extracted knowledge and the removal of noisy features. Their starting point is that there is no agreed definition of knowledge inside a network, so they adopt an interaction-based perspective supported by earlier mathematical evidence.

In this perspective, interactions serve as symbolic building blocks for inference patterns encoded by the model. The paper extends their definition so that interactions can be extracted from intermediate layers. This makes it possible to quantify which interactions newly appear and which disappear at each stage of forward propagation.

The resulting analysis connects layer-by-layer interaction changes with changes in generalization capacity and the instability of feature representations. Its contribution is a way to examine how internal information develops across depth, using an explicit mathematical representation of inference patterns. The conclusions concern knowledge as captured by these interactions, rather than resolving the broader question of how all neural-network knowledge should be defined.
icml-2024-layerwise-change-of-knowledge-.tldr: An extended interaction framework tracks which inference patterns emerge and disappear across a neural network’s layers.

paragraphs: Graph data presents a challenge for language models because relationships among nodes do not naturally fit a language-like input sequence. LLaGA addresses this mismatch by adapting graph information into a form a language model can use. The goal is to retain the model’s general-purpose capabilities while enabling it to work with graph structure.

The method reorganizes graph nodes into sequences that reflect their structure. A projector then maps these sequences into the token embedding space used by the language model. This creates an interface between graph representations and language-model processing, supporting graph tasks as well as explanations about graphs within one model.

Experiments cover four datasets and three tasks. The authors report that a single LLaGA model surpasses leading graph models in both supervised and zero-shot settings. They also report generalization to unseen datasets or tasks. Together, these findings support the usefulness of a shared graph-to-language interface for handling multiple graph problems, rather than requiring a separately specialized model for each evaluated setting.
icml-2024-llaga-large-language-and-graph.tldr: LLaGA maps structure-aware graph sequences into language-model embeddings, enabling one model to handle multiple graph tasks and explain graphs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback can reward longer answers even when their extra text is not helpful. A polished, verbose response may receive high scores from people, language-model evaluators, or reward models. ODIN studies this length-related reward hacking as a problem affecting both training and evaluation.

The authors first introduce an evaluation protocol that examines the trade-off between evaluation score and response length as training hyperparameters vary. Large-scale studies then investigate how training choices affect length bias. To modify the reward itself, they jointly train two linear preference-prediction heads: one encouraged to correlate with response length, and another encouraged to be decorrelated from it and focus more on content.

During reinforcement learning, the length-associated head is discarded. This removes the explicitly separated source of length reward from the training signal. Experiments report elimination of the reward’s correlation with length and a significant improvement in the resulting policy. The contribution combines a way to assess length-sensitive evaluation with a reward-model design intended to reduce that specific incentive.
icml-2024-odin-disentangled-reward-mitig.tldr: ODIN separates length-related reward from content-related preference to reduce verbosity-driven reward hacking in RLHF.

paragraphs: Diffusion models connect a complex data distribution with a simpler prior through a gradual process. Sampling can follow an ordinary differential equation, producing a trajectory from which a numerical solver constructs an output. This paper studies the structure of that trajectory and how understanding it can improve the choice of sampling times.

The authors characterize an implicit denoising trajectory and explain its role in shaping the coupled sampling trajectory. They identify strong regularity in trajectory shape regardless of the generated content. Based on this structure, they propose a dynamic-programming method for choosing a time schedule that better matches the path the sampler follows.

The scheduling strategy requires only small changes to an existing ODE-based numerical solver and adds negligible computational cost. The paper reports improved image-generation performance, especially when sampling uses five to ten function evaluations. This makes the trajectory analysis practically relevant: when only a few evaluations are available, better placement of those evaluations can improve the resulting generation without substantially changing the solver.
icml-2024-on-the-trajectory-regularity-o.tldr: Regularities in diffusion sampling trajectories motivate a low-cost time schedule that improves image generation with few solver evaluations.

paragraphs: Unlearnable examples aim to hinder unwanted learning from data by adding imperceptible perturbations. Existing approaches can depend on a particular dataset or on consistent labels, limiting how broadly the protection transfers. This paper proposes a universal perturbation generator designed around concepts, with the aim of extending unlearnability across datasets and labeling arrangements.

The method uses pretrained multimodal models to connect image data with text concepts in a shared embedding space. This connection allows image information to be expressed through text concepts. A concept-wise discriminant loss then guides alignment of the text embeddings as part of making the perturbed data difficult to learn from.

Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate cross-dataset transferability, utility without reliance on matching labels, and robustness against attacks. These are the properties the authors describe as concept unlearnability. The approach matters because it targets a more transferable unit of protection than a fixed dataset’s labels. The reported evidence supports broader applicability across the tested settings, rather than establishing that every possible learning or attack procedure will fail.
icml-2024-one-for-all-a-universal-genera.tldr: A multimodal perturbation generator targets concept-level unlearnability that transfers across datasets and does not depend on matching labels.

paragraphs: Operator learning builds models of mappings between functions, offering surrogate models for systems described by partial differential equations. Transformers have been adapted to this setting, but their self-attention can be computationally demanding and difficult to interpret. This paper asks whether a more suitable attention mechanism can exploit the spatial structure already present in these problems.

The Position-induced Transformer uses attention determined only by spatial relationships among the locations where input functions are sampled. Unlike conventional self-attention, this attention mechanism does not depend on the function values at those locations. Inspired by numerical PDE methods, it makes sampling geometry the basis for attention and substantially improves efficiency.

Across diverse PDE benchmarks, PiT outperforms leading neural operators on the evaluated operator-learning tasks. It also exhibits improved discretization convergence compared with the Fourier neural operator, addressing how the model behaves as the sampling discretization changes. These findings show that spatial relationships can provide a powerful basis for attention in this setting, alongside the practical benefit of reducing the computation associated with value-dependent attention.
icml-2024-positional-knowledge-is-all-yo.tldr: PiT uses sampling positions to determine attention, improving efficiency and performance on PDE operator-learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning considers how uncertainty in outcomes should affect decisions. This paper develops a distributional reinforcement-learning framework that supports general function approximation and a class of static Lipschitz risk measures. The scope of the theory is tied to that risk-measure class, allowing the authors to analyze learning efficiency under an explicit mathematical setting.

The framework includes two meta-algorithms. RS-DisRL-M uses a model-based approach with model-based function approximation, while RS-DisRL-V uses a model-free approach with general value-function approximation. New estimation methods based on least squares regression and maximum likelihood operate in distributional reinforcement learning with an augmented Markov decision process.

The authors derive a regret upper bound with square-root dependence on K, up to logarithmic factors, for the stated risk-sensitive setting. They also provide a framework for examining how estimation functions affect strategy effectiveness and sample complexity. The result is a theoretical contribution toward statistically efficient risk-sensitive learning, covering both model-based and model-free approaches under the specified assumptions on risk measures.
icml-2024-provable-risk-sensitive-distri.tldr: A distributional RL framework provides model-based and model-free risk-sensitive algorithms with a square-root regret dependence under static Lipschitz risk measures.

paragraphs: Learning PDE solutions across different geometries can require many geometry-solution training pairs. Producing those pairs is expensive when each simulation takes hours or days, as can happen in engineering design optimization. Reference Neural Operators address this data burden by organizing predictions around a known reference solution.

Given that solution, an RNO learns how the solution changes as the reference geometry is deformed. The learning target is the smooth dependence on geometric deformation. This gives the model a reference point from which to predict solutions for altered geometries, and the authors describe the approach as substantially more data efficient.

Experiments show that RNO can learn across different types and numbers of geometric objects using relatively small datasets. It outperforms the evaluated baselines in accuracy, with error reductions reaching 80%. These results support using reference solutions as a useful basis for geometry-dependent PDE prediction. The practical significance is greater accuracy with less training data in a setting where obtaining each additional solution can be costly.
icml-2024-reference-neural-operators-lea.tldr: Reference Neural Operators improve data efficiency by predicting how PDE solutions change when a geometry is deformed from a known reference.

paragraphs: Large-kernel convolutional networks have shown strong performance and efficiency, but their robustness has been less well understood. This paper investigates how they compare with conventional small-kernel networks and vision transformers. The question is both practical and explanatory: how well do these models withstand challenging inputs, and what properties accompany that behavior?

The authors evaluate robustness on six diverse benchmark datasets. They then use quantitative and qualitative experiments to investigate differences between large-kernel networks and typical convolutional networks. Their analysis examines occlusion invariance, kernel attention patterns, and frequency characteristics as sources of insight into the observed robustness.

The experiments show that purely convolutional networks can achieve robustness comparable to, and sometimes greater than, that of vision transformers. This is an empirical finding about the evaluated models and benchmarks. It demonstrates that strong robustness is attainable within a convolutional architecture and motivates closer attention to kernel size and the associated representation properties when studying why vision models remain reliable under difficult input conditions.
icml-2024-revealing-the-dark-secrets-of-.tldr: Large-kernel convolutional networks show robustness comparable to or better than vision transformers in a six-benchmark evaluation.

paragraphs: Some cooperative multi-agent problems contain Euclidean symmetries: different spatial arrangements can share the same underlying decision structure. This paper investigates how to exploit those symmetries in reinforcement learning. The aim is to make the model’s architecture reflect relationships already present in the task, giving learning a useful structural starting point.

The authors first characterize a subclass of Markov games with symmetries that admit symmetric optimal values and policies. This theoretical result motivates actor-critic neural networks with symmetry constraints embedded in their design. The constraints act as an inductive bias, guiding the networks toward behavior consistent with the relevant transformations.

Across cooperative multi-agent benchmarks, the resulting methods achieve better performance and strong generalization, including zero-shot and transfer learning in unseen scenarios with repeated symmetric patterns. The connection between theory and architecture is central: the symmetry constraints are motivated by properties established for a particular game class. The reported transfer benefits concern situations where those recurring patterns provide reusable structure for the agents’ decisions.
icml-2024-rm-e-3-equivariant-actor-criti.tldr: Symmetry-constrained actor-critic networks improve cooperative multi-agent learning and transfer in settings with recurring Euclidean structure.

paragraphs: A classifier’s uncertainty can be unreliable when an input differs from its training data. Improving this often requires additional out-of-distribution examples or an expensive ensemble. Split-Ensemble instead reorganizes the existing learning task to create diverse submodels that learn to recognize inputs outside their own assigned distributions.

The method divides the task into complementary subtasks using feature similarity. Each subtask treats one part of the available data as in distribution and the remainder as out of distribution. This supplies an OOD-aware training objective without collecting external OOD data. Iterative splitting and pruning create a tree-like architecture whose submodels share low-level features to avoid additional inference costs.

Experiments report accuracy gains over a single model of 0.8%, 1.8%, and 25.5% on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet. Corresponding mean AUROC gains for OOD detection are 2.2%, 8.1%, and 29.6%. The results support combining task diversity with shared computation: the evaluated system improves classification and uncertainty-based detection without the additional computational cost usually associated with an ensemble.
icml-2024-split-ensemble-efficient-ood-a.tldr: Split-Ensemble improves accuracy and OOD detection by creating complementary subtasks and sharing computation among their submodels.

paragraphs: Learning from sets requires combining information without making the result depend on the order of the elements. This paper proposes Quantile Pooling as a permutation-invariant way to perform that combination. It aims to retain both prominent features and information about the broader distribution of features within a set.

The motivation comes from complementary strengths of familiar pooling operations. Max pooling emphasizes salient features, while average pooling captures more of the overall distribution and subtle information. Quantile Pooling brings these properties together while remaining lightweight and fast. Across a variety of tasks, the authors show that it can outperform both alternatives in the areas where each is typically strongest.

The paper also introduces Stacked Deep Sets, a more expressive and universal variant of deep set networks. This architectural contribution uses depth to enhance learning, complementing the pooling operation’s balance of robustness and sensitivity. Together, the proposals address two parts of set modeling: what information survives aggregation and how effectively the network can transform that information through multiple layers.
icml-2024-stacking-deep-set-networks-and.tldr: Quantile Pooling combines salient and distributional set information, while Stacked Deep Sets adds depth for greater expressiveness.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models are increasingly used to scale language models, but their reliability has received less systematic assessment. They can also underperform dense models when adapted to new domains. MoE-RBench investigates this gap by comparing the two model families on reliability as well as their behavior under different training and inference choices.

The assessment covers three areas: safety and hallucination, resistance to adversarial attacks, and robustness to inputs outside the training distribution. The authors evaluate numerous models and datasets across these dimensions. This provides a way to examine whether an apparent advantage or weakness persists across different forms of reliability.

The empirical results suggest that mixture-of-experts models can be more reliable than dense language models when appropriate hyperparameters, training recipes, and inference techniques are used. The authors also find that robustness is sensitive to basic training settings. The implication is conditional: architecture alone does not determine the outcome, and successful adaptation depends on how the sparse model is trained and used.
icml-2024-textttmoe-rbench-towards-build.tldr: MoE-RBench finds that sparse expert models can outperform dense models in reliability, with outcomes strongly dependent on training and inference choices.

paragraphs: A neural architecture’s ability to represent arbitrary algorithms does not by itself explain which algorithms it readily learns. This paper investigates a more specific property of transformers: their ability to implement gradient-based learning under simple parameter configurations. The focus is on learning nonlinear functions from information provided in context.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that nonlinear transformers naturally learn to carry out gradient descent in function space. In this interpretation, the learning process adjusts a candidate function through successive improvements, providing a mechanism for nonlinear in-context learning. Their results cover a broad class of combinations of nonlinear architectures and nonlinear learning tasks.

The paper also finds that the optimal nonlinear activation depends naturally on the class of functions being learned. This connects an architectural choice to the structure of the target task. Together, the findings offer an algorithmic account of nonlinear in-context learning, grounded in both analysis and experiments. The account applies to the studied class of architecture-task combinations rather than asserting one mechanism for every transformer behavior.
icml-2024-transformers-implement-functio.tldr: Theory and experiments support functional gradient descent as a mechanism for nonlinear in-context learning in a broad class of transformers.

paragraphs: This paper studies what additional transformer depth makes possible by constructing sequence-learning tasks that separate different capabilities. The tasks examine memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization. This controlled design lets the authors connect attention-layer count to specific demands instead of treating all successful sequence prediction as the same kind of ability.

For the designed tasks, a transformer with one attention layer can perform well at memorization but struggles with the other capabilities. Reasoning and generalization require at least two attention layers in the analysis, while contextual generalization may require three. The latter is a qualified finding, and these depth conclusions are grounded in the paper’s task setting.

The authors also identify simple operations that one attention layer can perform. More complex tasks can be expressed as combinations of those operations, explaining how stacking layers can enable their solution. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. This compositional perspective offers a way to reason about depth and motivates studying whether similar decompositions illuminate more practical and complex tasks.
icml-2024-what-can-transformer-learn-wit.tldr: Designed sequence tasks reveal how stacking attention layers enables reasoning and generalization beyond what one layer achieves.
